questions.stemHtml: An intraoperative frozen section has been sent by a surgeon to the pathology laboratory. A special stain has been applied by the pathologist as empty looking areas were found after routine staining resulting in inability to make any diagnosis. Identify the special stain used?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Oil red “O”

 

  • Oil Red O is a fat-soluble dye that specifically stains neutral lipids and triglycerides red. It is commonly used in:
    • Frozen sections (because lipids are dissolved during paraffin processing)
    • Detection of fat embolism, fatty liver, liposarcomas, etc.
  • The frozen section shows empty-appearing spaces on routine H&E staining.
  • These spaces typically indicate the presence of lipids, which get dissolved during routine processing.
  • To confirm the presence of lipids, Oil Red O is used on fresh/frozen tissue.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hematoxylin: A routine nuclear stain; not specific for any pathological deposit.

 

Option C. Alizarin Red: Stains calcium deposits.

 

Option D. PAS with diastase: Stains glycogen and mucopolysaccharides; diastase digests glycogen.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the correctly matched option about the pattern of cell death and the DNA electrophoresis pattern shown?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Necrosis (A), Apoptosis(B), normal pattern (C)

 

In the given gel electrophoresis image:

 

  • Lane A shows a smear, typical of necrosis, where DNA is degraded randomly.
  • Lane B shows a ladder pattern, which is characteristic of apoptosis due to internucleosomal cleavage of DNA.
  • Lane C shows intact high molecular weight DNA, indicating normal cells without DNA fragmentation.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old female with a history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with joint pain and swelling. Laboratory investigations reveal elevated levels of anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA) and rheumatoid factor (RF). Imaging studies show erosions and deformities in the joints. Further investigation reveals activation of caspase-4 and release of IL-1β and IL-18 in the synovial fluid. Which of the following forms of regulated cell death is likely contributing to the joint inflammation and damage in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Pyroptosi

 

In rheumatoid arthritis (RA), chronic inflammation and immune-mediated damage to the joints occur. 

 

Clues in the Question:

 

  • Caspase-4 activation
  • Release of IL-1β and IL-18
  • Joint inflammation

 

Pyroptosis:

 

  • A form of regulated cell death characterized by:
  • Caspase-1, -4, or -5 (in humans) activation
  • Release of pro-inflammatory cytokines like IL-1β and IL-18
  • Cell swelling, lysis, and strong inflammatory response

 

Caspase-4 is specifically involved in non-canonical pyroptosis, particularly in response to intracellular LPS and DAMPs.

 

Pyroptosis is commonly seen in autoimmune diseases, including RA, due to chronic innate immune activation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Necroptosis: Involves RIPK1/RIPK3/MLKL pathway; also inflammatory but does not involve IL-1β or caspase-4.

 

Option C. Autophagy: A cell survival mechanism; not directly inflammatory.

 

Option D. Ferroptosis: Iron-dependent lipid peroxidation; not linked to IL-1β or caspases.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old male presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting. Serum amylase and lipase levels are significantly elevated. Abdominal CT scan reveals inflammation of the pancreas. Which of the following types of necrosis is commonly associated with acute pancreatitis?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans (d) Fat necrosis

questions.stem: Please read the statements carefully as this is an assertion and reason question Assertion (A): Necrotic cells have a moth eaten appearance when compared to normal cells in irreversible cell injury.Reason (R): There may be loss of nuclear material in irreversible cell injury

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are the true and Reason (R) is a correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are the true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false ​​​​​​​

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true

questions.answerText: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are the true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
questions.solutionHtml:
bsp;

Assertion (A):

 

  • "Necrotic cells have a moth-eaten appearance when compared to normal cells in irreversible cell injury."
  • True: Necrotic cells often appear vacuolated or fragmented (moth-eaten) due to disintegration of organelles and cytoplasm.

 

Reason (R):

 

  • "There may be loss of nuclear material in irreversible cell injury."
  • -Also True:  Irreversible injury leads to nuclear changes like karyolysis, karyorrhexis, and pyknosis.

 

Now the critical question is:

 

Does the loss of nuclear material directly cause the moth-eaten appearance of necrotic cells?

 

Not exactly. The moth-eaten appearance refers more to cytoplasmic and organellar disruption, including vacuolization and membrane breakdown.



ers more to cytoplasmic and organellar disruption, including vacuolization and membrane breakdown.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old male presents with progressive decline in his cardiac function and reduced work capacity. He expired and on autopsy, the microscopic examination of the cardiac tissue revealed a yellow-brown pigment deposited in the cardiac cells. Which of the following is true about the location of the pigment present in this individual?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Perinuclear, intralysosomal

 

The yellow-brown pigment described in this 70-year-old man’s cardiac tissue is lipofuscin, which accumulates with age or in conditions of "wear and tear" - especially in long-lived, post-mitotic cells like cardiac myocytes.

 

Key facts about lipofuscin:

 

  • Origin: Lipofuscin is derived from lipid peroxidation of subcellular membranes.
  • Location: It is stored in lysosomes, often appearing as perinuclear granules.
  • Nature: It is intracellular, perinuclear, and found within lysosomes (thus intralysosomal).

 

 

Ref: Robbins 10th edition page 65




Robbins 10th edition page 65

questions.stemHtml: A 30 year old lady gets pregnant after few years of her marriage. She delivers a healthy baby but has excessive post-partum hemorrhage due to which the obstetrician decides to perform a hysterectomy. The histological appearance of her uterine tissue is given alongside. Which of the following best describes the microscopic change in her uterus?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Hypertrophy

 

During pregnancy, the uterus enlarges significantly to accommodate the growing fetus. This increase in size is primarily due to:

 

Hypertrophy of smooth muscle cells — each individual myometrial (muscle) cell increases in size, not number.

 

Hyperplasia may also occur to a limited extent, but hypertrophy is the predominant change.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Dysplasia: Refers to disordered cell growth and is considered a premalignant change. This is not seen in normal pregnancy.

 

Option B. Metaplasia: This is the reversible transformation of one differentiated cell type to another. Not applicable here.

 

Option C. Hyperplasia: Although there may be some increase in cell number, hypertrophy predominates in the smooth muscle of the uterus during pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male presents with a high-grade fever, hypotension, and diffuse maculopapular rash. Laboratory tests reveal leucocytosis and thrombocytopenia. Blood cultures grow Gram-negative bacteria. Which of the following forms of regulated cell death is involved in the pathogenesis of sepsis-associated multiorgan dysfunction in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Pyroptosis

 

In rheumatoid arthritis (RA), chronic inflammation and immune-mediated damage to the joints occur. 

 

Clues in the Question:

 

  • Caspase-4 activation
  • Release of IL-1β and IL-18
  • Joint inflammation

 

Pyroptosis:

 

  • A form of regulated cell death characterized by:
  • Caspase-1, -4, or -5 (in humans) activation
  • Release of pro-inflammatory cytokines like IL-1β and IL-18
  • Cell swelling, lysis, and strong inflammatory response

 

Caspase-4 is specifically involved in non-canonical pyroptosis, particularly in response to intracellular LPS and DAMPs.

 

Pyroptosis is commonly seen in autoimmune diseases, including RA, due to chronic innate immune activation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Autophagy: A cell survival mechanism; not directly inflammatory.

 

Option B. Apoptosis: Programmed cell death via caspases (initiator caspase-8/9 → executioner caspase-3/6/7).

 

Option D. Necroptosis: Involves RIPK1/RIPK3/MLKL pathway; also inflammatory but does not involve IL-1β or caspase-4.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not correctly matched?

options.label: C
options.text: Ghost cells with tombstone appearance: coagulative necrosis

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Colliquative appearance: coagulative necrosis 

 

  • Colliquative necrosis is another name for liquefactive necrosis, not coagulative.
  • Seen in brain infarcts and abscesses where tissue becomes liquefied.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Soap formation: lipid digestion: Correct.

 

  • Soap formation (saponification) occurs in fat necrosis, especially in the pancreas.
  • Lipases break down fat into free fatty acids, which bind calcium to form chalky-white soaps.

 

Option B. Cheese like appearance: caseous necrosis: Correct. Caseous necrosis (e.g., in tuberculosis) has a cheesy, soft, white appearance due to the combination of coagulative and liquefactive necrosis.

 

Option C. Ghost cells with tombstone appearance: coagulative necrosis: Correct. Coagulative necrosis preserves the outline of cells (ghost cells), and tombstone appearance refers to preserved cell outlines with loss of nuclei, especially seen in early myocardial infarction.



ers to preserved cell outlines with loss of nuclei, especially seen in early myocardial infarction.

questions.stem: Which of the following is correct about hydroxyl free radical? Hydroxyl radical is the most powerful oxygen derived free radicalHydroxyl radical is generated from H2O2 by Fenton reactionHydroxyl radical is converted to water by glutathione peroxidaseCauses damage of lipids, proteins, and DNA
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. (b) Only 1, 2 and 4 are true

 

Glutathione peroxidase converts H2O2 (and not Hydroxyl radical) into water.

 

1. Hydroxyl radical is the most powerful oxygen-derived free radical: True. The hydroxyl radical (•OH) is highly reactive and damaging, making it the most dangerous among ROS (reactive oxygen species).

 

2. Hydroxyl radical is generated from H₂O₂ by Fenton reaction: True. This occurs when ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) reacts with hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) in the Fenton reaction, producing •OH: Fe2++H2​O2​→Fe3++⋅OH+OH−

 

4. Causes damage of lipids, proteins, and DNA: True. •OH causes:

 

  • Lipid peroxidation of membranes
  • Protein fragmentation and oxidation
  • DNA strand breaks and base modifications

 

Other Option:

 

3. Hydroxyl radical is converted to water by glutathione peroxidase: False. Glutathione peroxidase detoxifies hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) and lipid peroxides, not hydroxyl radicals directly.

 

Once •OH is formed, it's too reactive to be enzymatically neutralized—it must be prevented from forming in the first place.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old male with end-stage renal disease presents with joint pain and stiffness. Radiographic examination reveals extensive calcification of the articular cartilage in multiple joints, including the shoulders, hips, and knees. Which of the following types of calcification is most likely responsible for the findings in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Metastatic calcification

 

In this case, the patient has end-stage renal disease (ESRD) and presents with calcification in multiple joints. This pattern is most consistent with metastatic calcification, which refers to the deposition of calcium salts in normal tissues due to elevated serum calcium or phosphate levels.

 

Pathophysiology:

 

In ESRD:

 

  • Phosphate excretion is impaired, leading to hyperphosphatemia.
  • This causes secondary hyperparathyroidism, which increases bone resorption and raises serum calcium.
  • The elevated calcium-phosphate product precipitates in normal tissues, including:
    • Joints
    • Vessels
    • Lungs
    • Gastric mucosa

 

This process results in metastatic calcification, even in normal tissues.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Dystrophic calcification: Occurs in damaged or necrotic tissues despite normal serum calcium/phosphate.

 

Option C. Hyperplastic calcification: This is not a standard term in pathology.

 

Option D. Heterotopic calcification: Refers to bone formation in soft tissues, such as in myositis ossificans, not typical for ESRD-related calcification.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male presents with progressive weakness and atrophy of his upper and lower limb muscles. Electromyography reveals evidence of denervation, and a muscle biopsy shows the presence of intracellular protein aggregates. Which of the following proteases is primarily involved in the degradation of these protein aggregates?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans (d) Proteasomes

questions.stem: A 70-year-old male with a history of hypertension and diabetes presents with a non-healing ulcer on his right foot. Physical examination reveals an area of dry, black, and mummified tissue surrounded by healthy skin. Doppler ultrasound shows no blood flow in the affected area. Which of the following types of necrosis is most likely present in the ulcer?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Coagulative necrosis

 

This patient presents with:

 

  • A dry, black, mummified ulcer
  • No blood flow in the affected area (confirmed by Doppler)
  • A classic setting of ischemia due to vascular disease (from hypertension and diabetes)

 

These findings point to coagulative necrosis, specifically a dry gangrene, which is a clinical variant of coagulative necrosis.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Liquefactive necrosis: More common in brain infarcts or abscesses; involves enzymatic digestion leading to liquid tissue.

 

Option B. Caseous necrosis: Seen in tuberculosis; has a cheese-like gross appearance.

 

Option C. Fibrinoid necrosis: Seen in immune complex disease and malignant hypertension.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old female presents with recurrent episodes of abdominal pain and bloating, accompanied by diarrhea and constipation. Colonoscopy reveals evidence of inflammatory bowel disease, and a biopsy confirms the diagnosis of Crohn's disease. The genetic analysis revealed single nucleotide polymorphism in ATG16L1 gene. Which of the following cellular processes may play a role in the pathogenesis of this disease?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Autophagy

 

Single nucleotide polymorphism in ATG16L1 gene is associated with altered autophagy which is postulated to be important in the development of Crohn’s disease

 

Crohn's disease has a known association with mutations in genes involved in autophagy, particularly the ATG16L1 gene.

 

ATG16L1 (Autophagy Related 16 Like 1):

 

  • Plays a critical role in autophagy, a cellular process involved in:
    • Degradation and recycling of cellular components
    • Host defense (including the handling of intracellular pathogens in the gut)
    • Regulation of immune response

 

Mutations in ATG16L1 can impair autophagy, leading to:

 

  • Defective clearance of intracellular bacteria
  • Altered antigen presentation
  • Dysregulated inflammation — all of which contribute to the pathogenesis of Crohn’s disease

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Apoptosis: While cell death contributes to tissue damage, apoptosis is not primarily linked to ATG16L1 mutations.

 

Option B. Necrosis: Uncontrolled cell death; not associated with ATG16L1.

 

Option C. Ferroptosis: Iron-dependent form of cell death; not implicated in Crohn’s or ATG16L1 function.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about caspases?

options.label: B
options.text: Caspase 1, 4 and 5 are involved with release of interleukin 1

options.label: C
options.text: Caspase 10 is involved in initiation of intrinsic pathway of apoptosis

options.label: D
options.text: Caspase 9 is associated with increased mitochondrial permeability in apoptotic cell death

questions.answerText: Caspase 10 is involved in initiation of intrinsic pathway of apoptosis
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Caspase 10 is involved in initiation of intrinsic pathway of apoptosis

 

  • Caspase-10 is involved in the extrinsic (death receptor) pathway, not intrinsic.
  • It is similar to Caspase-8 and is activated by death receptors like Fas and TNFR.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Caspase 3 is an executioner caspase: True. 

 

  • Caspase-3 is a key executioner caspase in both intrinsic and extrinsic pathways.
  • It cleaves many cellular substrates to bring about the morphological and biochemical changes of apoptosis.

 

Option B. Caspase 1, 4, and 5 are involved with release of interleukin 1: True

 

  • These are inflammatory caspases.
  • Caspase-1 activates IL-1β and IL-18 via the inflammasome.
  • Caspase-4 and 5 (human) and Caspase-11 (mouse) are involved in non-canonical inflammasome activation and pyroptosis.

 

Option D. Caspase 9 is associated with increased mitochondrial permeability in apoptotic cell death: True.

 

  • Caspase-9 is activated by the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway.
  • Mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization leads to cytochrome c release, forming the apoptosome (Apaf-1 + cytochrome c + procaspase-9), activating caspase-9.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is Not associated with the histological finding shown in the image?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Multiple myeloma

 

Psammoma bodies are microscopic, round, concentrically laminated calcifications. They are typically seen in certain tumors and have diagnostic significance.

 

Associated conditions with psammoma bodies:

 

  1. Papillary thyroid carcinoma 
    • Classic association.
  2. Meningioma 
    • Commonly shows psammoma bodies.
  3. Mesothelioma 
    • May show psammoma bodies (especially in the papillary variant).
  4. Serous papillary cystadenocarcinoma of the ovary or endometrium 

 

C. Multiple myeloma 

 

Does NOT show psammoma bodies.

 

Characterized by plasma cell infiltration, Russell bodies, amyloid deposits, and bone lesions, but not concentric calcifications.
